title: Immune Responses in Reproductive Disease
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: The reproductive tract asks the immune system to do contradictory things: ignore sperm and a half-foreign fetus, arm the newborn with maternal antibody, and still defend mucosal surfaces against infection. This chapter explains how testicular immune privilege, fetal tolerance, placental IgG transfer, milk IgA, and the vaginal microbiota achieve this, and what happens when they fail: antisperm antibodies, autoimmune orchitis, Rh hemolytic disease, bacterial vaginosis, persistent HPV infection, and tubal scarring. Board questions typically give a clinical outcome such as infertility, hydrops, or ectopic pregnancy and ask for the immune mechanism behind it.

Histology of the seminiferous epithelium, cervix, vagina, and fallopian tube (RE-2)
Structure of the placenta and trophoblast layers (RE-1, RE-3)

connections.how: HPV E6 and E7 act on p53 and Rb only in infections that cell-mediated immunity fails to clear.
The organisms behind bacterial vaginosis, salpingitis, and cervical neoplasia are the same ones whose host responses this chapter explains.
Interactions between uterine NK cells and extravillous trophoblast shape spiral artery remodeling, which fails in preeclampsia.
Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn is an antibody-mediated extravascular hemolysis, detected by antiglobulin testing.
CD4 T cell loss in HIV allows HPV persistence, which is why invasive cervical carcinoma is an AIDS-defining illness.

terms.def: The capacity of a site, such as the testis or the maternal-fetal interface, to tolerate antigens that would trigger rejection elsewhere.
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells that seal meiotic and postmeiotic germ cells away from blood and lymph.
Antibodies against sperm surface antigens that agglutinate sperm and impair motility and fertilization.
Carrying antigens half from self and half from a genetically different individual, as the fetus does with paternal HLA.
A nonclassical, minimally polymorphic HLA class I molecule on extravillous trophoblast that engages inhibitory receptors on NK cells and T cells.
NK cell killing of cells that lack the class I molecules that normally engage NK inhibitory receptors.
The neonatal Fc receptor, an MHC class I-like molecule that binds IgG at acidic pH and transports it across the placenta.
Dimeric IgA carried across epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor and protected by the attached secretory component.
Passage of fetal red cells into the maternal circulation, most often at delivery.
Abnormal fluid in two or more fetal compartments (skin, pleura, pericardium, peritoneum), the end stage of severe fetal anemia or heart failure.
A vaginal squamous cell whose borders are obscured by an adherent coat of Gardnerella and other bacteria.
A self-assembled shell of viral capsid protein that mimics the virion surface but contains no viral genome.

sections.title: Testicular immune privilege and its failure

blocks.text: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty, long after central tolerance has been established in the thymus. Spermatocytes, spermatids, and sperm express new proteins that were never presented for deletion, so to the immune system they are foreign. The testis survives this through immune privilege, which has an anatomical layer and an active layer.

The anatomical layer is the blood-testis barrier. Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells, near their bases, divide the seminiferous epithelium into a basal compartment, which holds spermatogonia and is open to interstitial fluid, and an adluminal compartment, which holds spermatocytes and spermatids. Germ cells cross the junctions as new junctions form beneath them, so antigen-bearing cells never contact blood or lymph. The active layer is local immunosuppression: Sertoli cells, Leydig cells, and resident macrophages of a largely anti-inflammatory type release TGF-beta and IL-10, Sertoli cells express Fas ligand that can kill activated Fas-bearing T cells, intratesticular androgen dampens inflammation, and regulatory T cells restrain responses that do start. Active suppression matters because the barrier is weaker in the rete testis and excurrent ducts, where sperm antigens can leak.

blocks.title: Barrier breach to antisperm antibodies
steps: Trauma, torsion, vasectomy, or orchitis
Blood-testis barrier or duct wall is breached
Sperm antigens reach antigen-presenting cells
B cells make antisperm IgG and IgA
Sperm agglutinate and move poorly
Reduced fertility despite sperm production
blocks.caption: Antisperm antibodies follow any event that exposes sequestered sperm antigens to the systemic immune system.

blocks.text: After vasectomy, spermatogenesis continues; sperm that leak from the distended epididymis and vas are phagocytosed, and antisperm antibodies develop in most men. They matter when fertility is sought after reversal. Antibodies bound to sperm cause head-to-head or tail-to-tail agglutination, block penetration of cervical mucus, and interfere with the acrosome reaction and zona pellucida binding, so fertility falls even when the count is normal.

Mumps orchitis follows parotitis in a minority of postpubertal males. Viral replication causes interstitial inflammation and edema, and because the tunica albuginea cannot stretch, pressure injures the seminiferous tubules, which later atrophy. It is usually unilateral, so sterility is uncommon, but subfertility and antisperm antibodies can follow.

Autoimmune orchitis is T cell-mediated inflammation of the testis, isolated or with systemic autoimmunity (vasculitis, autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes). Tubular destruction lowers sperm output and Sertoli cell inhibin B, so FSH rises; if Leydig cells are lost, testosterone falls and LH rises. This is primary (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism.

blocks.title: Reading testicular injury from laboratory values
rows: Count often normal; agglutination, poor motility
blocks.caption: FSH tracks the seminiferous tubules through inhibin B; LH tracks Leydig cells through testosterone.

blocks.predict: After vasectomy reversal, semen contains sperm in normal numbers but they clump and swim poorly. What explains this?
blocks.explain: The vasectomy exposed sperm antigens and induced antisperm antibodies, which persist after the duct is reopened and agglutinate sperm.

sections.title: Maternal tolerance of the semiallogeneic fetus

blocks.text: Half of the fetal genome, including HLA alleles, comes from the father, so the fetus is a semiallogeneic graft that by ordinary rules should be rejected. It survives because the trophoblast, the fetal tissue that contacts maternal blood and decidua, presents little for maternal T cells to attack and actively inhibits maternal NK cells, and because the maternal response at the interface is regulated. Tolerance is local, not a general shutdown: many multiparous women make antibodies against paternal HLA, which shows the mother does see fetal antigens.

Villous syncytiotrophoblast, which is bathed in maternal blood in the intervillous space, expresses no classical HLA class I or class II, so maternal cytotoxic T cells find no paternal peptide-HLA complex to recognize. Extravillous trophoblast, which invades the decidua and remodels the spiral arteries, lacks the highly polymorphic HLA-A and HLA-B and all class II, but expresses HLA-C and the nonclassical molecules HLA-E and HLA-G. HLA-G is minimally polymorphic, so it offers few foreign epitopes.

Silencing class I creates a new risk, because natural killer (NK) cells kill cells that lack class I (missing-self recognition), and uterine NK cells are the most abundant leukocytes in early decidua. HLA-G engages inhibitory receptors such as LILRB1 (also present on T cells and macrophages), and HLA-E, which presents leader peptides derived from HLA-G and HLA-C, engages the inhibitory receptor CD94/NKG2A. Instead of killing, uterine NK cells secrete cytokines and angiogenic factors that help remodel spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels. Signaling between maternal NK receptors (KIR) and fetal HLA-C is thought to tune this remodeling, and inadequate remodeling is linked to preeclampsia (RE-13-H).

blocks.title: Layers of protection at the maternal-fetal interface
rows: No HLA-A, HLA-B, or class II on trophoblast
No target for maternal CD8 or CD4 T cells
HLA-G and HLA-E on extravillous trophoblast
Inhibit uterine NK cells; prevent missing-self killing
Complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) on trophoblast
Limit complement injury from any bound antibody
Tryptophan depletion suppresses local T cell proliferation
Limit recruitment of effector T cells into the decidua
blocks.caption: No single mechanism is sufficient; tolerance depends on concealment, inhibition, and regulation together.

blocks.text: The limits of this protection are clinically important. It shields the trophoblast, not fetal cells that leave the placenta: fetal red cells entering the maternal circulation are fully exposed, which is why maternal alloantibodies against red cell antigens can still cause disease (C04).

The newborn's adaptive immune system is naive, so for its first months it relies on antibody made by its mother. Two routes deliver it: IgG across the placenta before birth, giving systemic protection, and secretory IgA in milk after birth, protecting the gut surface.

The neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) is an MHC class I-like molecule paired with beta2-microglobulin. Syncytiotrophoblast takes up maternal plasma by fluid-phase endocytosis; as the endosome acidifies to about pH 6, FcRn binds the Fc region of IgG and carries it across the cell, releasing it at the neutral pH of the fetal side, while unbound proteins go to lysosomes. The same pH-dependent recycling protects IgG from degradation throughout life and gives most IgG a half-life of about 3 weeks. Placental transfer is active and selective: it begins near the end of the first trimester, rises steeply in the third, and at term cord IgG often equals or exceeds maternal IgG. IgG1 crosses most efficiently and IgG2 least, and very preterm infants are born with low IgG.

IgM, a pentamer of about 900 kDa, has no FcRn binding site, and IgA, IgD, and IgE do not cross either. Any IgM in cord or neonatal blood was therefore made by the fetus and means the fetus met an antigen in utero, as in congenital infection. Maternal IgG decays over months while the infant's own IgG production starts slowly, so total IgG reaches a low point at about 3 to 6 months (physiologic hypogammaglobulinemia).

FcRn cannot tell protective from harmful IgG. Maternal IgG autoantibodies and alloantibodies cause transient neonatal disease that fades as the IgG is cleared over weeks to months, a time course that itself identifies the mechanism.

blocks.title: What crosses and what it does
rows: Neonatal IgM is fetal; suggests congenital infection
Anti-D and other red cell IgG
Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
Mucosal protection in the infant gut
blocks.caption: Only IgG crosses the placenta, whether it is protective or pathogenic; IgA reaches the infant through milk.

blocks.text: Plasma cells in the lactating breast home there from gut-associated lymphoid tissue, so milk IgA targets organisms the mother has met in her own gut. Dimeric IgA joined by J chain is carried across mammary epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, and the retained secretory component resists digestion. Little is absorbed; it acts in the lumen by immune exclusion, binding microbes and toxins so they cannot attach. Milk also supplies lactoferrin, lysozyme, and oligosaccharides that act as decoy receptors.

blocks.title: Interpreting newborn serology
blocks.text: A healthy-appearing newborn has Toxoplasma IgG in cord blood but no Toxoplasma IgM. Step 1: IgG crosses by FcRn, so the IgG may be entirely maternal; it shows the mother was infected at some time, not that the infant was. Step 2: IgM cannot cross, so its absence means there is no evidence the fetus mounted its own response. Step 3: if the IgG is only maternal it will fall steadily over the following months, whereas an infected infant keeps or raises its titer. A positive Toxoplasma IgM in the neonate, by contrast, would point directly to congenital infection.

sections.title: Rh alloimmunization and hemolytic disease of the fetus

blocks.text: The D antigen of the Rh system (RhD) is a red cell membrane protein encoded by RHD. People who lack it, usually because both copies of RHD are deleted, are RhD-negative, about 15% of people of European ancestry and fewer in most other populations. RhD is strongly immunogenic, but unlike anti-A and anti-B, anti-D is not naturally present; it forms only after exposure to RhD-positive red cells through pregnancy or transfusion.

In pregnancy, exposure comes from fetomaternal hemorrhage. The largest bleed usually occurs at delivery, but miscarriage, induced abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis, abdominal trauma, and antepartum bleeding can also sensitize. The primary response is slow and mostly IgM, which cannot cross the placenta, and it usually develops after the first infant is born. That pregnancy is therefore usually spared, but memory B cells remain.

blocks.title: From sensitization to hydrops
steps: RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive fetus
Fetal red cells enter mother, usually at delivery
Primary IgM response and memory B cells
Later RhD-positive pregnancy recalls memory
Anti-D IgG crosses placenta by FcRn
Splenic macrophages destroy coated fetal red cells
Fetal anemia, extramedullary hematopoiesis, heart failure
Hydrops fetalis
blocks.caption: Sensitization in one pregnancy sets up antibody-mediated hemolysis in the next.

blocks.text: In a later RhD-positive pregnancy, even a small bleed recalls memory B cells, which now make class-switched IgG anti-D. FcRn carries it to the fetus, where it binds RhD on red cells. This is type II hypersensitivity, antibody against a fixed cell-surface antigen, not immune complex disease. Anti-D activates complement poorly, so destruction is mainly extravascular: fetal splenic macrophages bind the Fc portion of coated cells through Fc gamma receptors and phagocytose them.

Anemia drives erythropoietin release, so the marrow, liver, and spleen release nucleated red cells (erythroblastosis fetalis), and extramedullary hematopoiesis enlarges the liver and spleen. Severe anemia causes high-output heart failure, and hepatic hematopoiesis and congestion impair albumin synthesis and portal flow; together these produce hydrops fetalis. Before birth the placenta carries unconjugated bilirubin to the mother's liver. After birth the infant's immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase is overwhelmed, jaundice appears within the first day, and unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and stain the basal ganglia (kernicterus). The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive on the infant's red cells, and the indirect test detects anti-D in maternal serum.

blocks.title: Rh versus ABO hemolytic disease
rows: Group O mother, group A or B fetus
Preexisting IgG anti-A and anti-B in group O
Usually mild; jaundice more than anemia
Strong antigen; antibody bound only by red cells
A and B weak on fetal cells; antigen on other tissues absorbs antibody
blocks.caption: Both are type II hypersensitivity mediated by maternal IgG.

blocks.title: Why the first baby is spared and ABO mismatch protects
blocks.text: An RhD-negative, group O woman has had one RhD-positive baby. Step 1: sensitization needs fetal red cells in her circulation, usually at that delivery, and the response that follows is slow and mostly IgM, which does not cross the placenta, so the first baby escaped. Step 2: if that baby was group A, her natural anti-A would have destroyed the fetal cells before RhD was presented, making sensitization less likely. Step 3: if she was sensitized, memory B cells make IgG anti-D in the next RhD-positive pregnancy. Passive anti-D given at exposure works like step 2, clearing RhD-positive cells before a primary response; it cannot erase memory once formed.

The vagina is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Estrogen thickens it and loads the intermediate and superficial cells with glycogen. As cells shed, host alpha-amylase breaks glycogen into maltose and related sugars, which lactobacilli (mainly Lactobacillus crispatus, L. gasseri, L. jensenii, and L. iners) ferment to lactic acid. This keeps the pH at about 3.8 to 4.5 in reproductive-age women. Undissociated lactic acid inhibits anaerobes, Gardnerella, and many sexually transmitted pathogens. Lactobacilli also occupy epithelial binding sites, and some strains produce bacteriocins and hydrogen peroxide.

Cervical mucus, antimicrobial peptides (defensins, secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor, lactoferrin), and antibodies add protection. Secretory IgA is present, but unlike most mucosal surfaces the lower female genital tract also contains substantial IgG, much of it derived from serum.

Because the defense depends on estrogen, it is weak before puberty and after menopause, when the epithelium is thin, glycogen and lactobacilli are scarce, and the pH is above 4.5. Menstrual blood and semen, both near neutral or alkaline, raise the pH transiently.

blocks.title: Loss of lactobacilli to bacterial vaginosis
steps: Douching, new or multiple partners, menses
Lactobacilli and lactic acid decline
pH rises above 4.5
Gardnerella forms biofilm on epithelial cells
Anaerobes overgrow and produce amines
Clue cells, thin gray discharge, fishy odor
blocks.caption: Bacterial vaginosis is a shift in the whole community, not infection by a single new organism.

blocks.text: In bacterial vaginosis (BV), Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes such as Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Atopobium vaginae increase many-fold. Gardnerella biofilm coats squamous cells, producing clue cells. Anaerobes decarboxylate amino acids to amines (trimethylamine, putrescine, cadaverine) that raise the pH further; adding potassium hydroxide (KOH) volatilizes them, giving a fishy odor (whiff test). Bacterial sialidases degrade mucins and IgA. Neutrophils are few, so this is a vaginosis rather than a vaginitis. Loss of the acid barrier raises the risk of acquiring sexually transmitted infections including HIV, of pelvic inflammatory disease, and of preterm birth.

blocks.title: Vaginal pH and inflammation by cause
rows: Clue cells, positive whiff test, few neutrophils
Yeast tolerates acid; favored by antibiotics, high estrogen, diabetes
blocks.caption: A raised pH points toward loss of lactobacilli or trichomoniasis; candidiasis occurs at normal pH.

sections.title: Immunity to HPV and the L1 virus-like particle vaccine

blocks.text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus that reaches basal keratinocytes through microabrasions, especially at the cervical transformation zone. Its life cycle follows epithelial differentiation: basal cells keep the genome as an episome and express early proteins (E1, E2, E6, E7) at low levels, while the capsid proteins L1 and L2 are made only in upper differentiating layers, and virions are released as surface cells are shed.

This design hides the virus. There is no viremia and no cell lysis, so there is little inflammation; capsid antigen appears only in cells about to be lost; and E6 and E7 dampen interferon signaling. Natural infection therefore induces weak, inconsistent neutralizing antibody. Even so, most infections and low-grade lesions regress, usually within about 1 to 2 years, through cell-mediated immunity: Th1 CD4 T cells and cytotoxic CD8 T cells recognize early proteins such as E2, E6, and E7 on infected keratinocytes, and regressing lesions contain dense T cell infiltrates. Antibody cannot do this, because basal cells hold viral DNA inside the cell and display no capsid.

L1, the major capsid protein, self-assembles when expressed alone in yeast or insect cells into virus-like particles (VLPs). These display the conformational neutralizing epitopes of the virion but contain no DNA, so they cannot infect or transform. Given intramuscularly, their dense, repetitive surface strongly activates B cells, producing type-specific neutralizing IgG at titers well above those after natural infection. IgG transudates into cervical mucus and exudes at sites of microtrauma, where virions must first bind the basement membrane before entering basal cells, so the virus is neutralized before entry. The same logic makes the vaccine prophylactic only: it cannot reach an established infection. HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical carcinomas, and HPV 6 and 11 cause most anogenital warts.

blocks.title: Two arms of HPV immunity
rows: Early proteins (E2, E6, E7) in infected cells
Clears existing infection and low-grade lesions
Vaccine responses weaker at low CD4 counts
blocks.caption: Antibody prevents infection; T cells end it.

blocks.text: When CD4 T cells are depleted by HIV or T cell function is suppressed after transplantation, HPV infections persist, are often multiple and multifocal, and progress more often to high-grade CIN and invasive carcinoma, and anal and vulvar neoplasia rise as well. Persistence allows HPV DNA to integrate and E6 and E7 to disable p53 and Rb (RE-10). Invasive cervical carcinoma is an AIDS-defining illness.

blocks.predict: Would vaccine-induced anti-L1 antibody clear an existing low-grade cervical lesion?
blocks.explain: No. Infected basal cells carry viral DNA intracellularly and make no L1, so there is nothing for neutralizing antibody to bind; clearance needs T cells against early proteins.

sections.title: Salpingitis, tubal scarring, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy

blocks.text: Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars D to K) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infect columnar epithelium of the endocervix and can ascend through the endometrium to the fallopian tubes. Salpingitis is the central lesion of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Chlamydial infection is asymptomatic in most women, so it often goes untreated, persists, and recurs. Neither organism leaves durable protective immunity, partly because of antigenic variation (gonococcal pili and Opa proteins, chlamydial major outer membrane protein).

Most tubal damage comes from the host response rather than the organism. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium; infected epithelial cells release IL-1, IL-6, IL-8 (CXCL8), and TNF, recruiting neutrophils and then lymphocytes. Clearance requires a Th1 response with IFN-gamma, but that response also injures the mucosa. IFN-gamma induces indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, which depletes tryptophan; chlamydiae that cannot replicate enter a persistent form that continues to release antigens such as chlamydial heat shock protein 60 (HSP60). On reinfection, sensitized T cells respond faster and more strongly, so each episode does more harm, and antibodies to chlamydial HSP60 are associated with tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

N. gonorrhoeae attaches to nonciliated cells by pili and Opa proteins and passes through them. Ciliated cells are killed indirectly: released lipooligosaccharide (LOS) and peptidoglycan fragments induce TNF, which causes ciliated cells to slough. An intense neutrophilic exudate produces acute purulent salpingitis, and pus can leak from the fimbriae into the pelvis (pyosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess) or track to the liver capsule (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis).

blocks.title: Salpingitis to ectopic pregnancy or infertility
steps: Chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis, often silent
Ascent to the fallopian tube
Cytokines, neutrophils, and Th1 response injure mucosa
Ciliated cells lost; plicae fuse
Fibrosis and adhesions narrow or close the tube
Partial narrowing: embryo implants in tube
Complete blockage: hydrosalpinx, infertility
blocks.caption: The same scarring process produces ectopic pregnancy or tubal factor infertility depending on how much of the lumen remains.

blocks.text: Repair replaces mucosa with fibrous tissue. The plicae (mucosal folds) lose cilia and fuse, the lumen narrows, the fimbriae can close, and adhesions tether the tube to the ovary and pelvic wall. Complete distal occlusion with trapped fluid forms a hydrosalpinx and causes tubal factor infertility. Partial damage favors ectopic pregnancy: fertilization occurs normally in the ampulla, but lost cilia and a distorted lumen slow transport, so the blastocyst is still in the tube when it is ready to implant, about 6 to 7 days after fertilization. The risk of infertility rises with each episode of PID.

blocks.predict: Why does a woman with several past chlamydial infections have a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy than one with a single treated infection?
blocks.explain: Each reinfection meets sensitized T cells, producing a stronger inflammatory response and more cilia loss and fibrosis, which slows embryo transport.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on chlamydial pathogenesis and the flow.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology set the stage. Sertoli cell tight junctions, the layered trophoblast, the glycogen-rich vaginal epithelium, the transformation zone, and the ciliated tubal mucosa each determine where antigen is hidden, where it is exposed, and which cells an infection can reach. Biochemistry supplies the effectors: pH-dependent binding by FcRn, lactic acid from glycogen, amines from anaerobic metabolism, tryptophan depletion by indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, and bilirubin conjugation that the newborn liver cannot yet keep up with.

Immunology and pathology then explain the outcomes. Two kinds of tolerance appear here: sequestration with local suppression in the testis, and concealment with NK inhibition at the placenta. Both are local, so systemic responses still occur when antigen escapes, as in antisperm antibodies and Rh alloimmunization. Antibody and T cells divide the work against HPV, so a T cell deficit predicts persistence, while in the fallopian tube the T cell response that clears Chlamydia is itself the cause of scarring. Many details, such as the relative weight of each tolerance mechanism or the role of chlamydial HSP60, come from experimental and association studies and remain incompletely settled.

summary: Sperm antigens appear after central tolerance forms; Sertoli tight junctions and local TGF-beta, IL-10, Fas ligand, and regulatory T cells keep them tolerated.
Trauma, torsion, vasectomy, or mumps orchitis exposes sperm antigens, and antisperm antibodies agglutinate sperm and impair motility and fertilization.
Autoimmune orchitis is primary hypogonadism: tubular loss raises FSH through low inhibin B, and Leydig loss lowers testosterone and raises LH.
Trophoblast lacks HLA-A, HLA-B, and class II; extravillous trophoblast expresses HLA-G and HLA-E, which inhibit uterine NK cell missing-self killing.
FcRn binds IgG at acidic endosomal pH and releases it at neutral pH, so only IgG crosses the placenta; neonatal IgM is fetal and suggests congenital infection.
Milk secretory IgA from gut-derived plasma cells protects the infant gut by immune exclusion; maternal IgG wanes to a low point at about 3 to 6 months.
Rh disease is type II hypersensitivity: anti-D IgG from a sensitized RhD-negative mother causes extravascular fetal hemolysis, anemia, and hydrops; the first pregnancy is usually spared.
Estrogen-driven glycogen feeds lactobacilli that keep vaginal pH at or below 4.5; their loss allows Gardnerella and anaerobes, giving clue cells, amines, and pH above 4.5.
HPV L1 VLP vaccines induce neutralizing IgG that blocks entry; T cells clear established infection, so HIV and other T cell deficits raise cervical cancer risk.
Repeated chlamydial and gonococcal salpingitis destroys cilia and causes fibrosis, leading to ectopic pregnancy with partial narrowing and infertility with complete blockage.

verify: The share of men who develop antisperm antibodies after vasectomy is quoted from about 50% to 80%; the chapter says most men.
The importance of Sertoli cell Fas ligand in testicular immune privilege is debated in the experimental literature; confirm whether NABNE expects it.
Autoimmune orchitis as a component of autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes is described mostly for type 1; ovarian failure is far more common than testicular failure in these syndromes.

Decidual and placental mechanisms (LILRB1, CD94/NKG2A, KIR and HLA-C interactions, indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, decidual stromal cell chemokine silencing) come from immunology references and research literature; confirm the depth NABNE Part I expects.
Timing of FcRn transfer (start near 13 weeks) and whether term cord IgG exceeds maternal IgG vary somewhat between sources; values are stated as approximate.
The statement that cervicovaginal secretions contain substantial serum-derived IgG relative to secretory IgA follows mucosal immunology reviews; confirm against the expected reference.

The role of lactobacillus hydrogen peroxide in vivo is disputed (the vagina is largely hypoxic); lactic acid is now regarded as the main antimicrobial. The chapter lists hydrogen peroxide as a strain-dependent product only.
Atopobium vaginae has been reclassified as Fannyhessea vaginae; confirm which name NABNE uses.
The proportion of HPV infections cleared within 1 to 2 years (often quoted as about 90% by 2 years) and the share of cervical cancers due to HPV 16 and 18 (about 70%) are consensus approximations.
Risk of tubal infertility after one, two, and three PID episodes is quoted from older Scandinavian series (about 8%, 20%, and 40%); the chapter states only that risk rises with each episode.
The proportion of RhD-negative individuals (about 15% in people of European ancestry) varies by population and source.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: blood-testis-barrier (basal and adluminal compartments with Sertoli tight junctions) and fcrn-transcytosis (pH-dependent IgG transport across syncytiotrophoblast).
